fetched_contents.text: Demand Response and Time-Variable Pricing Programs Demand response (DR) is a short-term, voluntary decrease in electrical consumption by end-use customers that is generally triggered by compromised grid reliability or high wholesale market prices. In exchange for conducting (and sometimes just committing) to curtail their load, customers receive a rate discount, a bill credit or some other remuneration. The majority of U.S. utilities offer their commercial and industrial customers at least some kind of DR option. In addition, the country's seven independent system operators/regional transmission organizations (ISO/RTOs) each sponsor DR programs or enable owners of demand response capabilities to bid into their markets for energy, capacity or other grid-support services. Demand-response capabilities often involve the ability to reduce consumption or use a behind-the-meter generator to serve a load that otherwise would be served by the grid or some combination of the two. Search for DR and TVP Programs and Rates The Federal Energy Management Program developed profiles of demand response programs and time-variable rates throughout the United States. Time-variable pricing (TVP)—in which electricity prices vary at different times of day (and often seasonally)—is also widespread in the electricity markets. Most utilities offer at least one TVP option for any given customer class. These often include simple time-of-use (TOU) rates, where prices move at set times and amounts through the day—generally with an afternoon peak period, overnight off-peak hours, and two "shoulder" periods in the hours in between. Additional TVP types are: * Real-time pricing (RTP): The prices charged to customers closely match either the underlying wholesale electricity market or the utility's cost of production * Day-ahead hourly pricing: The provider publishes its prices (reflecting its cost of acquisition or production) for the following day * Block-and-index pricing (sometimes called block-and-swing pricing): A combination of fixed pricing and RTP (i.e., the customer locks in some of its load at fixed prices and faces market pricing for additional usage). There are other types of TVP, but most are variants of those listed above. DR programs and TVP arrangements reflect the dynamic nature of electricity availability, delivery, and production costs. These costs can vary significantly over time, even every few minutes. These programs provide incentives for electricity consumers to manage loads by encouraging load curtailment and/or shifting, thereby mitigating some of these fluctuations and risks. Customers stand to gain substantially from participating in DR and TVP options, especially if they can adjust their electricity usage occasionally in response to market signals such as DR event notifications or price fluctuations.

fetched_contents.text: Large-scale grid integration of residential thermal energy storages as demand-side flexibility resource: A review of international field studies Under a Creative Commons license Open access Highlights * • We review 16 international field studies testing mass integration of residential HVAC as flexible demand into power grids. * • Key benefits demonstrated in the field tests are congestion relief and imbalance reduction in distribution grids (by ⩾60%). * • Six large field studies favor real-time pricing (energy tariffs) for balancing supply and demand in smart grids. * • HVAC flexibility on fast time scales and at high levels of i-RES penetration has not yet been field-tested adequately. * • We recommend trading flexibility as a quality-differentiated service. Abstract Power imbalances from fluctuating renewable electricity generators are counteracted by often expensive flexibility services. Heating, cooling, and air-conditioning (HVAC) of buildings, or domestic power-to-heat (P2H), are end uses of electricity that allow flexible load patterns due to the inertia of an attached thermal storage while meeting their quality constraints. Compared to smart appliances or electric vehicle charging, P2H exhibits large and predictable capacities of demand response (DR), because buildings in many countries account for 30–40% of the final energy demand, a large part of which is thermal. Yet, its practical flexibility potential remains largely unknown: is DR from P2H a mature technology for mass usage; is it cost-efficient, socially attractive, and ready to make key contributions to flexibility comparable to backup generators or battery storage? In the present paper, we review recent international field studies that are paving the way from research to practice. These field trials include real customers but have a broader research focus and a wider outreach than rolling out a new DR tariff or program or a specific new technology for DR. Their experience mirrors the technology readiness beyond revenue or policy studies, optimization frameworks or laboratory-scale micro-grids. We analyze the adequacy of the pricing mechanisms deployed for incentivization and remuneration and review the coordination mechanisms for balancing on different timescales including fast ancillary services. We conclude that current control and information technology and economic and regulatory frameworks which have been field-tested do not yet meet the flexibility challenges of smart grids with a very Flexible loads in demand response are represented as controllable, dispatchable resources whose consumption can be scheduled to avoid or shift load during constrained periods. The evidence indicates that flexible load resources are characterized by diverse types, small capacity, and wide distribution [N1-R5], which implies that modeling must accommodate heterogeneous appliances and equipment with different response characteristics. In practical terms, flexible loads include residential and commercial HVAC, thermal storage systems, smart appliances, and other controllable end-use devices that can adjust consumption in response to signals [N4-R3][N4-F2]. The field study review on residential HVAC emphasizes that buildings possess high amounts of flexible load and can contribute to smart grid stability by adjusting heating, ventilation, and air conditioning demand [N4-F2].

Parameterization of flexible loads typically involves defining consumption profiles, operating constraints, and dispatch variables. The modeling literature cited here describes optimization methods that prioritize energy storage resources and optimize load scheduling by prioritizing energy storage resources, enhancing system efficiency, reducing operating costs, and improving system efficiency [N1-R2]. Another study states that a mathematical model can quantify control parameters for optimum demand response and decide which resources to switch and when [N1-R1]. This implies that flexible loads are parameterized through switching decisions, time-of-use behavior, and resource-specific operational rules. The HVAC field study further notes that residential HVAC flexibility on fast time scales and at high levels of i-RES penetration has not yet been field-tested adequately [N4-F2], suggesting that parameterization must also account for time-scale mismatch and forecasting uncertainty.

Time-varying constraints and operational limits are captured through scheduling and dispatch formulations that explicitly model load bounds, device limits, and state transitions. The CPLEX-based model for heavy industrial load management determines the optimal power response allocation for each device across time periods [N1-R4], showing that operational limits are encoded as device-specific constraints. The optimization-oriented literature also suggests that stochastic programming and mixed-integer programming are used to model uncertainty and discrete decisions [N2-R2][N2-R3]. The field study review on HVAC and thermal energy storages further explains that flexibility services such as P2H allow flexible load patterns because buildings have attached thermal storage and must meet quality constraints [N4-F2]. This means that operational limits include both technical device limits and quality-of-service constraints, such as temperature setpoints or comfort thresholds.

Scheduling decisions are linked to consumption profiles and dispatch through optimization frameworks that couple load decisions with energy use and grid service. The evidence shows that flexible load scheduling is used to optimize load profiles, reduce operating costs, and improve system efficiency [N1-R2]. The HVAC review also indicates that real-time pricing and other field studies are used to coordinate balancing on different timescales [N4-F2]. More generally, the optimization literature points to convex relaxation, stochastic programming, and mixed-integer formulations as methods for integrating load dispatch with uncertainty and constraints [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R3]. Thus, scheduling decisions are not treated as independent from consumption; instead, they are embedded in a dispatch formulation that determines when and how much load to shift, curtail, or reschedule to align with cost, reliability, and operational goals.

Optimization in demand response reduces consumer charges and energy use by aligning load decisions with cost signals, price volatility, and grid service requirements. The evidence shows that demand response is often framed as a short-term voluntary decrease in consumption triggered by compromised grid reliability or high wholesale market prices, with customers receiving remuneration or rate discounts in exchange [N3-F1]. At the same time, time-variable pricing programs vary prices at different times of day and seasonally, and many include time-of-use (TOU), real-time pricing (RTP), and day-ahead hourly pricing [N3-F1]. These pricing structures create a direct link between consumer behavior and savings: customers can reduce consumption during expensive periods or shift load to cheaper periods [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R4].

Optimization objectives balance cost, load, and grid service by minimizing expenses while improving system efficiency and reducing peak demand. The cited optimization literature explicitly states that demand response strategies can reduce operating costs and improve system efficiency [N1-R2]. The IEA overview also emphasizes that demand response is established to motivate changes in electric use in response to changes in electricity prices [N5-R4]. This dual objective of cost minimization and service provision is reinforced by the field study review, which notes that demand-side flexibility services such as P2H can relieve congestion and reduce imbalance in distribution grids [N4-F2]. In other words, optimization does not simply minimize charges; it also supports grid stability and reliability through load management, which is critical when renewable generation is intermittent and system balancing becomes more difficult [N4-F2].

A major tradeoff is between shifting load, reducing peak, and saving money. The evidence indicates that dynamic pricing and demand response programs encourage load curtailment and shifting to mitigate fluctuations and risks [N3-F1]. However, shifting load may not always be the most economically attractive option if the consumer has limited flexibility or if the price signal is too volatile. The paper on dynamic pricing determines the price volatility necessary for automatic load shifting to cover the cost of smart metering within a household [N3-R1], showing that savings depend on both price signal strength and consumer investment in measurement and control. The same evidence also suggests that consumers can save money by taking advantage of lower-cost, off-peak billing and actively curbing energy usage [N3-R5]. This means that peak reduction and money saving are not always perfectly aligned: a consumer may reduce peak demand but still face higher costs if the price signal is weak or if the load shift is not well timed [N3-R1][N3-R5].

Pricing structures influence consumer behavior and savings by creating incentives to respond to market signals. The IEA notes that demand response is based on price-based programs, which use price signals and tariffs to incentivize changes in consumption [N5-R3]. The Department of Energy explains that time-variable pricing is widespread because electricity prices vary at different times of day and seasonally, and that most utilities offer at least one TVP option [N3-F1]. These structures shape consumer behavior by making expensive periods more costly and cheaper periods more attractive. The field study review further states that six large field studies favored real-time pricing for balancing supply and demand in smart grids [N4-F2], underscoring that pricing mechanisms are a key driver of consumer responsiveness. Overall, the evidence supports a balanced view: optimization reduces consumer charges and energy use by aligning load decisions with price signals, but the effectiveness depends on the strength of the price signal, the consumer’s responsiveness, and the system’s ability to support timely and accurate dispatch [N3-F1][N3-R1][N4-F2].

Practical barriers and implementation considerations for flexible load management include technical limitations, forecasting uncertainty, and behavioral response uncertainty, as well as the influence of market and program rules on feasibility and participation. The evidence indicates that flexible load control and forecasting face limitations because residential HVAC flexibility on fast time scales and at high levels of i-RES penetration has not yet been field-tested adequately [N4-F2]. This suggests that real-time or ultra-short-term control remains technically challenging, and forecasting accuracy is especially important when renewable generation is intermittent and demand response must be dispatched quickly [N4-F2]. The CPLEX-based industrial load model also shows that optimal power response allocation depends on precise device-level constraints and scheduling across time periods [N1-R4], implying that forecasting and control must resolve both temporal and device-specific uncertainty.

Participant incentives and behavioral response uncertainty are significant because consumers may not always respond as expected to price signals or demand response events. The two-stage demand response market mechanism paper explains that baseline estimation errors and strategic misreporting can lead to overpayments or underpayments, and that consumers may strategically misreport baselines or costs to improve their own utilities [N5-F4]. This directly points to the uncertainty that program designers face: even if a market mechanism is well designed, participants may not behave in the intended way, which can undermine the effectiveness of demand response. The HVAC field study review similarly notes that current control and information technology and economic and regulatory frameworks do not yet meet the flexibility challenges of smart grids with a very high share of intermittent renewable generation [N4-F2]. That means behavioral uncertainty is not just a consumer issue; it is also a system issue because demand response performance depends on both consumer willingness to act and the ability of the system to observe and reward that action.

Market and program rules affect feasibility and participation by shaping the terms under which consumers can participate and be remunerated. The demand response literature indicates that DR programs often involve monetary compensation, rate discounts, bill credits, or other remuneration, and that some programs are structured around participation incentives such as dynamic pricing or real-time pricing [N3-F1][N3-R5]. The two-stage mechanism paper also shows that settlement rules matter because credits are calculated based on reported baselines and costs, and the mechanism must ensure incentive compatibility so consumers report truthfully [N5-F4]. Meanwhile, the IEA notes that demand response markets are expanding but that greater effort is needed to align with the Net Zero Scenario [N5-F3]. This implies that program rules must not only be attractive to participants but also scalable and aligned with broader system goals. The field study review further highlights that current control and information technology and regulatory frameworks have not yet met the flexibility challenges of high renewable penetration, suggesting that market rules must evolve alongside technological and operational capabilities [N4-F2].

Taken together, the evidence shows that implementation barriers are multidimensional. Technical limitations constrain how precisely load can be controlled and predicted, behavioral uncertainty makes consumer responses unpredictable, and market rules determine whether participation is feasible and economically attractive. These barriers collectively mean that demand response cannot be treated as a purely algorithmic problem; it must also be embedded in a broader system of incentives, communication, and operational support [N4-F2][N5-F4][N5-F3].

However, shifting load may not always be the most economically attractive option if the consumer has limited flexibility or if the price signal is too volatile. The paper on dynamic pricing determines the price volatility necessary for automatic load shifting to cover the cost of smart metering within a household [N3-R1], showing that savings depend on both price signal strength and consumer investment in measurement and control.

The same evidence also suggests that consumers can save money by taking advantage of lower-cost, off-peak billing and actively curbing energy usage [N3-R5]. This means that peak reduction and money saving are not always perfectly aligned: a consumer may reduce peak demand but still face higher costs if the price signal is weak or if the load shift is not well timed [N3-R1][N3-R5]. In short, optimization must balance immediate cost savings with long-term system stability and grid service requirements.

### 6) How pricing structures influence consumer behavior and savings

Pricing structures are a central driver of consumer behavior and savings. The IEA notes that demand response is based on price-based programs, which use price signals and tariffs to incentivize changes in consumption [N5-R3]. The Department of Energy explains that time-variable pricing is widespread because electricity prices vary at different times of day and seasonally, and that most utilities offer at least one TVP option [N3-F1]. These structures shape consumer behavior by making expensive periods more costly and cheaper periods more attractive.

The field study review further states that six large field studies favored real-time pricing for balancing supply and demand in smart grids [N4-F2], underscoring that pricing mechanisms are a key driver of consumer responsiveness. Overall, the evidence supports a balanced view: optimization reduces consumer charges and energy use by aligning load decisions with price signals, but the effectiveness depends on the strength of the price signal, the consumer’s responsiveness, and the system’s ability to support timely and accurate dispatch [N3-F1][N3-R1][N4-F2].

## Practical barriers and implementation considerations

Practical barriers and implementation considerations show that flexible load management is not purely algorithmic; it is constrained by **technical limitations, forecasting uncertainty, and behavioral response uncertainty**, as well as the influence of **market and program rules** on feasibility and participation.

### 7) Technical limitations of flexible load control and forecasting

Technical limitations include the difficulty of controlling and forecasting flexible loads at fast time scales and under high renewable penetration. The HVAC field study review states that residential HVAC flexibility on fast time scales and at high levels of i-RES penetration has not yet been field-tested adequately [N4-F2]. This implies that real-time or ultra-short-term control remains technically challenging, and forecasting accuracy is especially important when renewable generation is intermittent and demand response must be dispatched quickly [N4-F2]. The CPLEX-based industrial load model also shows that optimal power response allocation depends on precise device-level constraints and scheduling across time periods [N1-R4], implying that forecasting and control must resolve both temporal and device-specific uncertainty.

### 8) Participant incentives and behavioral response uncertainty

Participant incentives and behavioral response uncertainty are significant because consumers may not always respond as expected to price signals or demand response events. The two-stage demand response market mechanism paper explains that baseline estimation errors and strategic misreporting can lead to overpayments or underpayments, and that consumers may strategically misreport baselines or costs to improve their own utilities [N5-F4]. This directly points to the uncertainty that program designers face: even if a market mechanism is well designed, participants may not behave in the intended way, which can undermine the effectiveness of demand response.

The HVAC field study review similarly notes that current control and information technology and economic and regulatory frameworks do not yet meet the flexibility challenges of smart grids with a very high share of intermittent renewable generation [N4-F2]. That means behavioral uncertainty is not just a consumer issue; it is also a system issue because demand response performance depends on both consumer willingness to act and the ability of the system to observe and reward that action.

### 9) How market and program rules affect feasibility and participation

Market and program rules affect feasibility and participation by shaping the terms under which consumers can participate and be remunerated. The demand response literature indicates that DR programs often involve monetary compensation, rate discounts, bill credits, or other remuneration, and that some programs are structured around participation incentives such as dynamic pricing or real-time pricing [N3-F1][N3-R5]. The two-stage mechanism paper also shows that settlement rules matter because credits are calculated based on reported baselines and costs, and the mechanism must ensure incentive compatibility so consumers report truthfully [N5-F4].

Meanwhile, the IEA notes that demand response markets are expanding but that greater effort is needed to align with the Net Zero Scenario [N5-F3]. This implies that program rules must not only be attractive to participants but also scalable and aligned with broader system goals. The field study review further highlights that current control and information technology and regulatory frameworks have not yet met the flexibility challenges of high renewable penetration, suggesting that market rules must evolve alongside technological and operational capabilities [N4-F2].

## Integrated conclusion

In summary, flexible loads are modeled in demand response as **controllable, dispatchable resources** whose consumption can be scheduled to avoid or shift load during constrained periods. They are parameterized through consumption profiles, operational constraints, and dispatch variables, and their time-varying behavior is captured through scheduling and dispatch formulations that include device-specific limits, quality-of-service constraints, and uncertainty-aware optimization methods [N1-R5][N4-R3][N4-F2][N1-R2][N1-R1][N1-R4][N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R1].

Optimization reduces consumer charges and energy use by aligning load decisions with cost signals, price volatility, and grid service requirements [N3-F1][N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R4]. It balances cost, load, and grid service, while the tradeoff between shifting load, reducing peak, and saving money depends on price signal strength, consumer responsiveness, and system dispatch capability [N1-R2][N5-R4][N4-F2][N3-R1][N3-R5]. Pricing structures are a central driver of consumer behavior and savings, with time-variable pricing and real-time pricing shown to encourage load curtailment and shifting [N3-F1][N4-F2].

Practical barriers include technical limitations, forecasting uncertainty, and behavioral response uncertainty, as well as market and program rules that affect feasibility and participation [N4-F2][N1-R4][N5-F4][N3-F1][N5-F3]. These barriers show that demand response cannot be treated as a purely algorithmic problem; it must also be embedded in a broader system of incentives, communication, and operational support [N4-F2][N5-F4][N5-F3].

Overall, the evidence supports a unified view: flexible load modeling in demand response is about making controllable loads responsive to market signals and system needs, while optimization turns that responsiveness into measurable reductions in energy use and consumer charges [N1-R1][N1-R2][N3-F1][N4-F2][N5-F4].
